'''Reference Re Senate Reform''' [2014] 1 S.C.R. 704, 2014 SCC 32<ref>{{Cite web |title=Reference re Senate Reform - SCC Cases |url=https://decisions.scc-csc.ca/scc-csc/scc-csc/en/item/13614/index.do |access-date=2025-10-22 |website=decisions.scc-csc.ca}}</ref> was a [[reference question]] to the [[Supreme Court of Canada]] regarding the [[Constitution of Canada|constitutional]] validity of proposals to change the Senate, such as term limits, consultative elections, and abolition. The ruling was announced April 2014, following arguments made in November 2013. The court decided that term limits and consultative elections could not be done by the [[Government of Canada|Federal Government]] alone through [[Parliament of Canada|Parliament]], but also required the consent of seven provinces representing more than 50% of the population, in accordance with the lower of two thresholds for the [[Amendments to the Constitution of Canada#Amendment formula|constitutional amending formula]].<ref name="Canadian Press" /><ref name="Maclean's piece">{{cite web | url=http://www.macleans.ca/politics/did-the-supreme-court-just-kill-senate-reform/ | title=Did the Supreme Court just kill Senate reform? | publisher=[[Maclean's]] | date=25 April 2014 | accessdate=20 November 2015 | author=Macfarlane, Emmett}}</ref> The court also ruled that Senate abolition would require the higher threshold for amendment: Parliamentary approval plus consent of all ten provinces.<ref name="Canadian Press">{{cite web | url=http://www.macleans.ca/politics/ottawa/high-court-says-no-to-unilateral-senate-reform/ | title=High court says no to unilateral Senate reform | publisher=[[Canadian Press]] | work=[[Maclean's]] | date=25 April 2014 | accessdate=20 November 2015}}</ref><ref name="Maclean's piece" />
